claims.text: What the strip looks like Polymorphic VT whose QRS amplitude twists around the baseline, arising with a prolonged QT.
claims.quote: Torsades de Pointes: Polymorphic VT with QRS amplitude that twists around the baseline; arises in the setting of prolonged QT.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) QRS: rapid, irregular complexes that appear to twist around the baseline
claims.quote: It is characterized by rapid, irregular QRS complexes, which appear to be twisting around the electrocardiogram (ECG) baseline.

claims.text: Rate: about 200–250 — too fast to perfuse
claims.quote: TdeP VT often causes syncope because the underlying rate (200 to 250 beats/minute) is nonperfusing.

claims.text: QT: prolonged — the diagnosis needs both polymorphic VT and QT prolongation
claims.quote: For TdP to be diagnosed, the patient must have evidence of both PVT and QT prolongation

claims.text: Onset: a PVC on the preceding T wave (“R on T”), often after a short-long-short R-R sequence (“pause dependent”)
claims.quote: TdP is initiated when a PVC occurs during the preceding T wave, known as ‘R on T’ phenomenon The onset of TdP is often preceded by a sequence of short-long-short R-R intervals, so called “pause dependent” TDP, with longer pauses associated with faster runs of TdP

claims.text: Warning signs: T-U fusion (sometimes giant TU waves), post-extrasystolic repolarization changes, visible T-wave alternans, frequent polymorphic PVCs (often bigeminy), repeated short runs of polymorphic VT
claims.quote: T-wave and U-wave fusion (sometimes with giant TU waves) Post-extrasystolic changes in repolarization pattern Macroscopic T-wave alternans (visible alternation of two different appearing T-waves) Frequent polymorphic ventricular premature beats representing single beats of TdeP (often in bigeminy) Repetitive short runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

claims.text: Pitfall: in short runs or a single-lead strip the twisting may not be apparent
claims.quote: During short runs of TdP or single lead recording the characteristic “twisting” morphology may not be apparent

claims.text: Runs at > 220/min last longer and are more likely to degenerate into VF
claims.quote: TdP with heart rates > 220 beats/min are of longer duration and more likely to degenerate into VF

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: ion-channel malfunction prolongs repolarization (long QT) and causes early after-depolarizations — seen as tall U waves, and as PVCs once they reach threshold
claims.quote: A prolonged QT reflects prolonged myocyte repolarisation due to ion channel malfunction This prolonged repolarisation period also gives rise to early after-depolarisations (EADs) EADs may manifest on the ECG as tall U waves; if these reach threshold amplitude they may manifest as premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)

claims.text: The long QT can be acquired, congenital, or both
claims.quote: The long QT interval responsible for torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia (TdeP VT) can be acquired, congenital or a combination.

claims.text: Risk depends on how long the QTc is, particularly > 0.50 seconds
claims.quote: The risk of TdeP VT is dependent on the degree of QTc prolongation, particularly if it is > 0.50 seconds.

claims.text: Most common acquired trigger: a QT-prolonging drug, especially a class Ia, Ic or III antiarrhythmic; also tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, some antivirals and antifungals
claims.quote: The most common predisposing factor in acquired TdeP VT is a QT interval–prolonging medication, especially a class Ia, class Ic, or class III antiarrhythmic medication Other medications that can induce TdeP VT include tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, and certain antivirals and antifungals

claims.text: Other predisposing factors: female sex, older age, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypothyroidism, slow or irregular ventricular rate, major acute brain injury
claims.quote: Female sex Older age Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Hypothyroidism Slow ventricular rate Irregular ventricular rate Major acute brain damage (eg, bleeding, stroke, traumatic brain injury)

claims.text: Causes combine — e.g., hypokalemia can precipitate torsades in congenital long QT syndrome
claims.quote: QT prolongation may occur secondary to multiple drug effects, electrolyte abnormalities and medical conditions; these may combine to produce TdP, e.g. hypokalaemia may precipitate TdP in a patient with congenital long QT syndrome

claims.text: Symptoms Syncope (the rate doesn't perfuse); palpitations are common in conscious patients
claims.quote: TdeP VT often causes syncope because the underlying rate (200 to 250 beats/minute) is nonperfusing. Palpitations are common among patients who are conscious.

claims.text: Often self-terminating, but it may degenerate into VF and cause sudden death
claims.quote: Because the QT interval shortens with increased ventricular rates, TdeP VT is often self-terminating. However, it instead may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and cause sudden death.

claims.text: Treatment Episode causing hemodynamic compromise: unsynchronized cardioversion, biphasic 120–200 J (or monophasic 360 J); early recurrence is the rule
claims.quote: An acute episode prolonged enough to cause hemodynamic compromise is treated with unsynchronized cardioversion, beginning with biphasic 120 to 200 joules (or monophasic 360 joules). Nevertheless, early recurrence is the rule.

claims.text: Correct electrolytes and give magnesium: fix hypokalemia; magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1–2 minutes, with a second bolus in 5–10 minutes if needed
claims.quote: Electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypokalemia), which can exacerbate the risk of ventricular arrhythmias, should be corrected. Patients often respond to magnesium, usually magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1 to 2 minutes. If this treatment is unsuccessful, a second bolus is given in 5 to 10 minutes

claims.text: Stop the causative drug and shorten the QT: raising the heart rate with temporary pacing and/or IV isoproterenol is often effective
claims.quote: If a medication is the cause, it is stopped, but until medication clearance is complete, patients with frequent or long runs of TdeP VT require treatment to shorten the QT interval. Because increasing the heart rate shortens the QT interval, temporary pacing, IV isoproterenol, or both are often effective.

claims.text: Long-term: avoid conditions that prolong the QT
claims.quote: Long-term treatment is avoidance of conditions that prolong the QT interval.
